symptoms: Normal leaf color and appearance
Normal stem and stalk characteristics
Normal tassel and silk characteristics
Normal ear and kernel appearance
Healthy root characteristics
Normal growth characteristics

Vibrant green color appropriate to hybrid
Vigorous early root development
Erect and sturdy stalk formation

Proper tassel development and uniform pollen shed
Synchronized silk emergence
Full kernel set with appropriate dry-down
causes: Optimal environmental conditions
Proper agricultural practices
Balanced soil fertility
Adequate moisture management

Use of certified disease-free and high-quality seeds
Proper field sanitation and residue management
Balanced fertilization based on soil tests
nutrition_recommendations: Apply nitrogen in split applications to prevent leaching
Ensure adequate phosphorus for early root development
Maintain optimal potassium levels for stalk strength and water regulation
Monitor secondary nutrients and micronutrients like zinc and sulfur

Monitor for early signs of nutrient deficiencies or pest incursions
Assess plant population density and uniform growth distribution

symptoms: Small, powdery pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules are dark cinnamon-brown early in the season
Pustules turn black late in the season as teliospores form
Severe infections cause leaf chlorosis and premature death
early_stage: Small, elongated chlorotic flecks on leaves
Development of raised, circular to elongated brown pustules (uredinia)
advanced_stage: Pustules rupture to release powdery brown urediniospores
Pustules coalesce, covering large leaf areas
Leaves yellow, wither, and dry up prematurely
Pustules turn black (telia stage)
causes: Fungal spores wind-blown from southern overwintering areas
Presence of susceptible corn hybrids
favorable_conditions: Extended periods of leaf wetness (6-8 hours)
spread_method: Wind-blown urediniospores travelling long distances
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids
Manage planting dates to avoid peak spore periods
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides if disease thresholds are breached prior to tasseling
organic_control: Use resistant varieties
Application of copper-based formulations or sulfur products early in infection cycles
chemical_control: Foliar fungicide applications should follow registered product labels and local regulations
Apply when pustules appear on lower leaves before the tasseling stage if weather forecasts predict persistent cool, wet conditions
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain balanced nitrogen and potassium levels to mitigate stress and support plant defense mechanisms
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid overhead irrigation in the late afternoon or evening to minimize the duration of leaf wetness
monitoring: Scout fields prior to tasseling, paying close attention to lower and mid-canopy leaves for early pustule development
economic_importance: Can cause significant yield losses (10-20%) in susceptible hybrids due to reduced photosynthetic area and premature senescence.
diagnosis_notes: Distinguished by pustules occurring on BOTH sides of the leaf, which are circular to elongate and break through the epidermis.

symptoms: Small, circular, light orange to reddish-brown pustules
Pustules occur predominantly on the UPPER leaf surface
Pustules are densely crowded and smaller than common rust
Severe infections lead to rapid leaf necrosis and lodging
early_stage: Tiny, light-green to yellow flecks on upper leaf surface
Small, raised orange pustules that remain covered by the epidermis longer than common rust
advanced_stage: Massive accumulation of orange spores on upper leaves
Pustules break through, causing extensive leaf bleaching and death
Stalk tissue becomes brittle, leading to severe lodging
causes: Spores carried by wind from tropical and subtropical regions annually
spread_method: Wind-borne urediniospores
prevention: Select highly resistant hybrids
Plant early in the season to evade late-summer spore clouds
treatment: Timely application of preventative and systemic foliar fungicides
organic_control: Genetic resistance is the primary organic control method
chemical_control: Apply fungicides promptly upon detection, adherence to local pesticide regulations is mandatory
nutrition_recommendations: Ensure sufficient potassium levels to strengthen cellular structures against rapid fungal penetration
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid excessive overhead irrigation that extends humidity periods in warm conditions
monitoring: Intensify scouting after pollination during warm, humid weather, focusing on the upper canopy where spores land
economic_importance: Extremely destructive; can cause up to 50% yield loss in susceptible hybrids under optimal conditions due to rapid defoliation.
diagnosis_notes: Pustules are smaller, more circular, dusty orange, and occur almost exclusively on the upper leaf surface, unlike common rust.

pathogen: Exserohilum turcicum (Pass.) K.J. Leonard & S.G. Suggs
symptoms: Large, long, elliptical, grayish-green to tan lesions
Lesions resemble 'cigar' shapes, measuring 2 to 15 cm
Dark fungal sporulation forms in the center of lesions under moist conditions
Lesions coalesce, causing extensive blighting of the canopy
early_stage: Small, water-soaked spots on lower leaves
Spots elongate into narrow, tan, linear stripes
advanced_stage: Classic large, cigar-shaped necrotic lesions spanning across veins
Massive leaf tissue death, giving fields a frosted or burned appearance
causes: Fungus overwinters as mycelium and conidia in infected corn debris
favorable_conditions: Prolonged leaf wetness (6-18 hours) from rain, dew, or fog
spread_method: Conidia spread locally by rain splash and wind over longer distances
prevention: Utilize resistant hybrids containing Ht genes or quantitative resistance
Implement a 1-2 year crop rotation away from corn
Deep tillage to bury infected crop residues
treatment: Foliar fungicides applied from tasseling (VT) through silking (R1) if economic thresholds are met
organic_control: Resistant varieties
Rigorous crop rotation
Decomposition of surface crop residue via tillage
chemical_control: Fungicides must be applied in accordance with local regulatory guidelines when lesions appear on leaves below the ear leaf prior to silking
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain adequate, balanced fertilization; avoid extreme nitrogen excess which can encourage dense vegetative growth that traps humidity
irrigation_recommendations: Manage pivot irrigation to minimize prolonged periods of continuous leaf wetness, avoiding night applications
monitoring: Scout weekly starting from mid-vegetative stages, looking at lower leaves first where residue contact occurs
economic_importance: Significant yield reductions occur if lesions develop on or above the ear leaf before or during silking.
diagnosis_notes: Characterized by the distinctive large, long, cigar-shaped tan lesions that are not bounded by leaf veins.

symptoms: Small, elongated, tan to brown lesions with parallel sides
Lesions are bounded by leaf veins, distinctively rectangular
Lesion size varies (2-3 cm long)
Race T causes severe ear rot and stalk lesions, while Race O is primarily foliar
early_stage: Small, oval, water-soaked spots on leaves
Development of light tan center with reddish-brown borders
advanced_stage: Lesions elongate into distinct rectangular shapes
Coalescence of lesions causes extensive leaf drying
Race T infections show dark, moldy growth on ears and stalk rotting
causes: Fungus overwinters in infested corn residue as mycelium or conidia
spread_method: Wind and splashing rain moving conidia up the plant canopy
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids (avoid Texas male sterile cytoplasm for Race T)
Crop rotation with non-grass species
Tillage to incorporate crop residue into the soil
treatment: Foliar fungicide application if disease is identified early on susceptible lines
organic_control: Selection of resistant cultivars
Burying crop residues immediately after harvest
chemical_control: Apply registered fungicides according to label directions and regional compliance criteria
nutrition_recommendations: Balanced macronutrient applications to prevent early tissue senescence which predisposes plants to infection
irrigation_recommendations: Schedule irrigation to allow leaves to dry fully during daylight hours
monitoring: Scout fields in warm, wet weather during mid-to-late vegetative stages, focusing on lower leaves
economic_importance: Historically devastating (1070s epidemic due to Race T); currently well managed via resistance but remains a threat in warm, humid regions.
diagnosis_notes: Lesions are smaller and more rectangular (parallel sides) than Northern Corn Leaf Blight, restricted by veins.
references: FAO Plant Production and Protection Series

symptoms: Distinct rectangular, blocky, tan to gray lesions
Lesions are strictly bounded by lateral veins
Lesions measure 1-6 cm long and 2-4 mm wide
Gray, cloudy appearance when fungus is actively sporulating
early_stage: Small, tan, circular to oval spots with yellow halos
Spots begin to take on a square or rectangular orientation as they hit leaf veins
advanced_stage: Perfectly rectangular, long gray-tan lesions running parallel to veins
Severe blighting, leaf death, and subsequent stalk lodging due to carbohydrate depletion
causes: Fungus overwinters in corn debris on the soil surface, particularly in conservation tillage systems
favorable_conditions: High relative humidity (over 90% for extended periods)
Frequent overcast days and prolonged leaf wetness
spread_method: Wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia from surface residues
prevention: Select hybrids with strong genetic tolerance or resistance scores
Rotate away from corn for a minimum of one to two years
Conventional tillage to degrade surface residue layers
treatment: Timely foliar fungicide application at VT-R1 stage if field thresholds are exceeded
organic_control: Strict crop rotation
Debris shredding and inversion tillage to enhance microbial breakdown of residue
chemical_control: Fungicide timing is critical; apply between VT and R1 when weather favors disease and susceptible hybrids are used, adhering to local laws
nutrition_recommendations: Ensure proper nitrogen-to-potassium ratios to enhance plant structural integrity and defense synthesis
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid frequent, light overhead irrigations; instead, apply water deeply and less frequently to minimize humidity duration
monitoring: Scout closely starting at V12 through silking; check the lower leaves for characteristic rectangular spots
economic_importance: One of the most economically damaging foliar diseases of corn globally, capable of causing 10-40% yield loss through rapid loss of photosynthetic capacity.
diagnosis_notes: The strictly rectangular shape with perfectly straight, vein-limited edges is diagnostic for Gray Leaf Spot.

symptoms: Oval to spindle-shaped lesions, tan to brown with dark reddish-brown borders
Lesions often appear first on lower leaves early in the season
Black, hair-like structures (setae) visible in lesion centers with magnification
May cause premature yellowing of lower leaves
early_stage: Small, water-soaked, circular spots on young leaves
Spots develop a yellow halo and dark margins
advanced_stage: Lesions enlarge up to 1-2 cm, becoming spindle-shaped
Coalescing lesions cause extensive leaf tip necrosis and drying
Presence of black fruiting bodies (acervuli) with bristly setae
causes: Fungus overwinters in infested corn residue on or near the soil surface
favorable_conditions: Extended periods of high humidity and rainy weather
spread_method: Conidia are spread primarily by splashing rain and wind
prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids
Implement crop rotation with non-hosts like soybeans
Incorporate residue via tillage to speed decomposition
treatment: Foliar fungicides are rarely economical specifically for the leaf blight stage but can reduce late-season stalk rot risk
organic_control: Crop rotation
Deep plowing
Maintaining balanced soil health to reduce early stress
chemical_control: Chemical control is typically restricted to high-value seed production fields, following registered local labels
nutrition_recommendations: Provide adequate early nitrogen and phosphorus to ensure vigorous seedling establishment and reduce stress susceptibility
irrigation_recommendations: Ensure proper field drainage to minimize pooling and excessive humidity within the seedling canopy
monitoring: Examine seedling and early vegetative corn fields for lower leaf spots, especially after early rainy spells
economic_importance: Usually minor on field corn as a foliar blight, but indicates the presence of the pathogen which can lead to severe stalk rot later.
diagnosis_notes: Look for spindle-shaped lesions with dark borders and microscopic black hairs (setae) in the center.
references: Purdue University Extension Entomology & Plant Pathology

symptoms: Shiny, linear black streaks or blotches on the outer stalk surface
Internal pith becomes disintegrated, dark brown, and shredded
Top-dieback, where the plant above the ear dies prematurely while lower parts remain green
Severe stalk lodging and breakage below the ear
early_stage: Narrow, water-soaked linear lesions on the stalk epidermis after pollination
Premature yellowing or death of the top leaves (top-dieback)
advanced_stage: Extensive shiny black coloration covering entire internodes
Stalk internal cavity becomes hollowed, pith turns dark and stringy
Stalk structural collapse (lodging) rendering mechanical harvesting difficult
causes: Systemic movement of the fungus within the plant or infection through the stalk/leaf sheaths from overwintered residue
favorable_conditions: Cloudy weather, low solar radiation during grain fill
High yield stress paired with stalk carbohydrate depletion
spread_method: Fungal spores enter through roots, wounds, or insect feeding sites, spreading systemically
prevention: Select hybrids with specific stalk rot and anthracnose resistance scores
Manage plant populations to avoid high density lodging stress
Control insect pests that wound stalks
treatment: Foliar fungicides applied at VT/R1 can indirectly reduce stalk rot by preserving leaf area and preventing carbohydrate depletion
organic_control: Burying crop residue
Strict crop rotation
Optimizing plant populations to reduce crowding stress
chemical_control: No direct curative chemical treatment for infected stalks; preventative foliar treatments follow registered local regulations
recommended_insecticides: Pyrethroids or Bt traits for stalk borers to prevent physical wounding
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain optimal potassium levels; balance nitrogen to prevent excessive late-season vegetative growth without sufficient stalk strength
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid drought stress during the grain filling period to prevent the plant from cannibalizing stalk carbohydrates
monitoring: Perform the stalk push test or pinch test on 100 plants per field mid-to-late season to assess lodging risk
economic_importance: A major cause of lodging and harvest losses globally; can cause up to 40% harvest efficiency loss and direct grain reduction due to premature death.
diagnosis_notes: Identified by the distinct, glossy black vertical blotches on the external stalk rind and dark shredded internal pith.
references: University of Illinois Extension Field Crop Reports

symptoms: Numerous small, circular, translucent spots (1-4 mm diameter)
Spots have a tan to cream center, surrounded by a distinct brown or purple ring
A prominent yellow chlorotic halo surrounds the outer ring
Lesions can coalesce, causing large areas of leaf necrosis under severe pressure
early_stage: Tiny, water-soaked circular spots on lower leaves
Appearance of a clear or translucent center in the spots
advanced_stage: Massive quantities of eye-like lesions covering the entire leaf blade
Premature leaf drying and death, resembling frost damage
Early senescing of the crop
causes: Fungus overwinters in un-decomposed corn residue left on the soil surface
spread_method: Rain splash and localized wind movement spreading conidia upward
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids
Implement crop rotation with non-grass species for at least one year
Clean plowing to bury infested plant residue
treatment: Foliar fungicide applications are effective if applied early in severe cases, primarily on susceptible inbreds
organic_control: Deep tillage
Crop rotation
Using certified clean seed stocks
chemical_control: Apply registered fungicides when economic thresholds are met, following local regulations and label restrictions
nutrition_recommendations: Ensure adequate, balanced fertility to maintain plant vigor, avoiding late nutrient deficiencies that accelerate tissue decline
irrigation_recommendations: Minimize nighttime overhead irrigation to reduce continuous leaf wetness periods in cool seasons
monitoring: Scout cool-season early plantings during late vegetative stages, focusing on lower leaves for the diagnostic halos
economic_importance: Usually minor in most commercial fields, but can cause notable localized losses in cool, wet northern corn-growing regions under continuous no-till.
diagnosis_notes: Characterized by very small, uniform, circular spots with a dark ring and a bright yellow halo, resembling an 'eye'.
references: Iowa State University Extension Path Report

symptoms: Formation of prominent, fleshy galls on infected tissues
Galls are initially covered by a shiny white to silvery-gray membrane
Internal gall tissue transforms into a powdery mass of black teliospores
Galls rupture to release black spores; leaf infections show small hard galls
early_stage: Small, white, swelling bumps or distortions on rapidly growing plant tissues
Galls feel soft and fleshy to the touch
advanced_stage: Galls enlarge significantly, up to 10-15 cm on ears or stalks
The outer silvery membrane dries, thins, and ruptures
Release of millions of powdery, dark black teliospores that stain the plant
causes: Fungus overwinters as teliospores in soil or crop debris, surviving for several years
favorable_conditions: Dry conditions during pollination followed by rain
Physical wounding caused by hail, high winds, insect feeding, or mechanical cultivation
spread_method: Wind-borne teliospores and water splash entering through wounds or silk channels
prevention: Plant hybrids with good resistance profiles
Avoid mechanical injury to plants during cultivation
Maintain balanced soil fertility
Control insect pests to minimize physical wounds
treatment: Foliar fungicides are completely ineffective and not recommended for common smut control
organic_control: Manual removal and destruction of young galls before they rupture (practical for small scales)
Crop rotation to lower local spore loads
chemical_control: No direct registered chemical control for field crops; focus entirely on genetic resistance and avoiding injury
recommended_insecticides: Insecticides targeting early season stalk and ear borers to limit entry wounds
nutrition_recommendations: Avoid excessive nitrogen applications, which create lush, soft tissues highly susceptible to infection; ensure adequate phosphorus
irrigation_recommendations: Provide consistent irrigation during pollination to prevent drought stress and subsequent silk exposure issues
monitoring: Check fields during late vegetative and reproductive stages for silver galls, especially after severe weather events like hail
economic_importance: Usually causes minor yield losses (under 2%) globally, though individual fields with severe ear infections can experience significant grain quality and yield drops. In some cultures, young galls are consumed as a delicacy (huitlacoche).
diagnosis_notes: Unmistakable due to large, fleshy, silver-white galls that mature into black, powdery spore masses on any above-ground plant part.

symptoms: Complete replacement of the tassel or ear with a dark, powdery spore mass
Absence of silks on infected ears
Infected tassels display a teardrop shape and fail to shed pollen
The spore mass is initially enclosed by a fragile membrane that breaks quickly, exposing stringy vascular bundles
early_stage: Systemic infection is invisible until flowering
Emerging tassels or ears appear abnormally thickened, compact, or deformed
advanced_stage: Tassel and ear structures are completely destroyed and replaced by black teliospores
Vascular strands remain as black, thread-like structures within the spore mass
Severe plant stunting or proliferation of leafy structures in the tassel (phyllody)
causes: Fungal spores present in the soil infect the corn seedling systemically through the roots during early germination
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry soils (21-28°C) during seedling emergence and early growth
spread_method: Soil-borne spores infect seedlings; spores are moved between fields by contaminated machinery
prevention: Plant highly resistant corn hybrids
Use systemic fungicidal seed treatments
Sanitize farm machinery when moving from infested to clean fields
treatment: Foliar fungicides are ineffective; management depends entirely on preventative seed treatments and resistance
organic_control: Strict long-term crop rotation out of fields with known infestation
Sanitation of tools and machinery
chemical_control: Apply registered systemic seed treatments prior to planting; comply with all local chemical regulations
nutrition_recommendations: Promote rapid early seedling growth with appropriate starter fertilizers containing readily available phosphorus
irrigation_recommendations: Maintain adequate soil moisture during planting and emergence to avoid dry conditions that favor root infection
monitoring: Scout fields during tassel and ear emergence to identify and map areas of infection for future management decisions
economic_importance: Can cause severe localized losses because infected plants produce zero grain. It is a regulated quarantine pest in some regions.
diagnosis_notes: Differs from common smut by infecting ONLY the reproductive structures (ears/tassels), leaving thread-like vascular fibers, and lack of fleshy silver galls.
references: EPPO Data Sheets on Quarantine Pests

symptoms: Individual or scattered small clusters of kernels exhibit white-to-pink or lavender mold
Infected kernels often show a diagnostic 'starburst' pattern (white streaks radiating from the silk attachment point)
Can affect any part of the ear, frequently associated with insect or bird damage
Production of dangerous mycotoxins (fumonisins)
early_stage: Faint white fungal mycelium appearing between kernels on scattered areas of the cob
Light pink discoloration of individual kernel crowns
advanced_stage: Extensive pinkish-white mold covering large blocks of kernels
Kernels become brittle, cracked, and thoroughly decayed
High accumulation of fumonisin mycotoxins within the grain
causes: Fungus overwinters in crop residue and enters the ear systemically via the roots/stalk or directly through the silk channel
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather during and after pollination
High temperatures (26-32°C) coupled with late-season insect damage or mechanical wounding
spread_method: Airborne or water-borne conidia landing on silks; systemic movement within the vascular system; insect vectors (e.g., earworms)
prevention: Select hybrids with genetic resistance and tight husk coverage
Utilize Bt traits to significantly reduce insect feeding wounds
Manage harvest timing to avoid late-season field drying if rot is present
treatment: Foliar fungicides targeting silks can provide partial suppression but must be paired with insect management
organic_control: Strict insect control using organic methods
Timely harvest
Proper drying and storage below 15% moisture
chemical_control: Fungicide applications at silking must follow local registration and are mostly applied in high-value production
recommended_insecticides: Pyrethroids or Bt traits to control ear-wounding insects like Helicoverpa zea
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain optimal nutrient balances to ensure uniform flowering and rapid husk development, reducing exposure windows
irrigation_recommendations: Manage irrigation to prevent late-season stress which predisposes maturing ears to fungal colonization
monitoring: Scout fields at physiological maturity (black layer) by peeling back husks on 100 ears to check for pink mold and starburst patterns
economic_importance: Highly important due to both direct yield reduction and strict regulatory limits on fumonisin mycotoxins in food and livestock feed.
diagnosis_notes: Look for the classic white 'starburst' streaks on individual, scattered pinkish kernels, rather than continuous mats of mold.

symptoms: Distinctive reddish-pink to bright pink mold growth
Infection characteristically begins at the TIP of the ear and progresses downward
Husk leaves may become tightly cemented to the ear by the pink mycelium
Production of hazardous mycotoxins including deoxynivalenol (vomitoxin) and zearalenone
early_stage: Fine pinkish mold visible at the absolute tip of the ear shortly after silking
Slight water-soaked appearance of tip kernels
advanced_stage: Brilliant deep-pink or red mat of mycelium engulfing the upper half or entirety of the ear
Husks glued tightly to the cob; kernels heavily decayed and soft
High concentration of vomitoxin rendering grain toxic to livestock (especially swine)
causes: Fungus overwinters on corn and small grain residues, producing perithecia that release airborne ascospores
favorable_conditions: Cool, wet, and humid weather within 3 weeks after silking (R1)
spread_method: Airborne ascospores and rain-splashed conidia entering directly through the wet silk channel
prevention: Select hybrids with high resistance scores and upright ear traits that drain well
Avoid rotating corn immediately after small grains like wheat
Tillage to bury crop residue and enhance degradation
treatment: Foliar fungicides applied precisely during early silking (R1) can provide suppression
organic_control: Crop rotation with non-hosts (e.g., soybeans)
Immediate drying of grain post-harvest to below 14% moisture
Deep burial of residues
chemical_control: Fungicides must be applied at the correct growth stage (R1) following local pesticide rules and restrictions
nutrition_recommendations: Ensure balanced fertility to avoid delayed or uneven silking across the field, which prolongs the infection window
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid overhead irrigation during peak silking to reduce water accumulation in the silk channel
monitoring: Scout fields prior to harvest, pulling back husks at the ear tip to check for reddish-pink mycelial progression
economic_importance: Critically high economic impact due to the severe effects of vomitoxin and zearalenone on animal health, causing feed refusal and reproductive failures.
diagnosis_notes: Identified by the dark pink-to-red mold color and its definitive progression from the ear tip downward, unlike Fusarium ear rot.

symptoms: Thick, dense, white-to-grayish mold growing between kernels
Infection characteristically starts at the BASE of the ear and moves upward
Entire ear can become structurally light, shriveled, and completely brown
Small, black, pinhead-sized fruiting bodies (pycnidia) embedded in the cob matrix or kernels
early_stage: Premature bleaching or yellowing of the ear husks while the rest of the plant remains green
Thin layer of white mycelium at the base of the ear
advanced_stage: The entire ear is encased in a dense, felt-like white mold mat
Ears are incredibly light, rotten, and break easily
Black pycnidia appear on the husks and dark kernel surfaces
causes: Fungus overwinters as pycnidia on corn stalks and residue left on the soil surface
favorable_conditions: Warm, wet weather with frequent, heavy rainfall during the first 2-3 weeks post-silking
Continuous corn cultivation under conservation tillage
spread_method: Rain splash dispersing conidia from surface residues directly onto the base of the ear or leaf axil
prevention: Select resistant hybrids
Implement a minimum 1-year crop rotation out of corn
Utilize clean tillage to bury infected stalk debris
treatment: Foliar fungicides generally offer very limited to no control for Diplodia ear rot; prevention is key
organic_control: Crop rotation
Deep plowing to eliminate surface inoculum sources
Harvesting early to prevent further rot progression
chemical_control: No highly effective post-emergence chemical control available for field applications; follow local label updates
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain standard balanced crop nutrition to prevent premature plant stress during early ear development
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid heavy overhead irrigation during early reproductive stages if continuous corn residue is present
monitoring: Look for early bleached husks in the field 2-4 weeks after silking; pull husks back to check for base-upward white mold
economic_importance: Can cause catastrophic localized yield losses and extreme grain dockage due to high percentages of damaged kernels, though it does not produce major toxins of human concern in North America (can cause diplodiosis in livestock in Africa).
diagnosis_notes: Distinguished by the dense white mold starting at the BASE of the ear, bleached husks, and tiny black pycnidia, with zero pink coloration.

pathogen: Aspergillus flavus Link; Aspergillus parasiticus Speare
symptoms: Powdery, olive-green to yellow-green mold growth on kernels
Typically associated with the tip of the ear or around insect wounds
Kernels may be shriveled, discolored, and easily broken
Production of aflatoxins, which are highly carcinogenic liver toxins
early_stage: Fine, yellowish-green dusting of spores on scattered kernels near the ear tip
Minor kernel discoloration
advanced_stage: Thick, powdery, olive-green mold coating large sections of the ear
Extensive grain decay
Extremely high levels of aflatoxin contamination exceeding regulatory safety limits
causes: Fungus survives in soil, crop debris, and organic matter; spores are highly robust and drought-tolerant
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (above 30-35°C) during pollination and grain fill
spread_method: Wind-borne conidia entering via silks or physical wounds caused by insects, birds, or hail
prevention: Select drought-tolerant hybrids with excellent husk coverage
Utilize insect-resistant Bt traits to eliminate wounding pathways
Apply competitive non-toxigenic biological control strains to the soil
treatment: No effective foliar chemical treatment; maximize post-harvest drying speed and cool storage
organic_control: Minimize drought stress via irrigation where possible
Rapid mechanical drying to under 13% moisture within 24 hours of harvest
chemical_control: No standard curative chemical control available for fields; compliance with strict local regulations regarding aflatoxin limits is required
recommended_insecticides: Pyrethroids or Bt traits to manage corn earworm, fall armyworm, and western bean cutworm
nutrition_recommendations: Ensure adequate potassium and nitrogen to mitigate heavy drought and temperature stress impacts on the crop
irrigation_recommendations: Critically important: Provide adequate irrigation during pollination and grain fill stages to alleviate the drought stress that triggers aflatoxin production
monitoring: Prioritize scouting in hot, dry areas; check ear tips for characteristic olive-green powder before harvest
economic_importance: Extremely high economic risk; even minimal aflatoxin contamination (above 20 ppb in the US for human food) can cause complete rejection of the grain lot, leading to severe financial loss.
diagnosis_notes: The distinct olive-green, powdery appearance of the mold combined with hot, dry field conditions is diagnostic.

pathogen: Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum (Cobb) Saaltink et al.
symptoms: Narrow, linear, light tan to brown streaks running parallel between leaf veins
Lesions have highly irregular, wavy, or jagged margins
A distinct, bright yellow chlorotic halo is highly visible when backlit
Lesions can measure from less than 1 cm to several centimeters long
early_stage: Small, water-soaked, translucent linear streaks on lower leaves
Development of early yellow halos around the streaks
advanced_stage: Streaks elongate and coalesce into broad bands of necrotic tissue
Considerable loss of green leaf area, spreading up into the high canopy
causes: Bacterium overwinters in infected crop residue and enters plants through natural openings (stomata) or wounds
spread_method: Rain splash, wind-driven rain, and overhead irrigation water moving bacteria across leaves
prevention: Select tolerant hybrids
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops (e.g., soybeans or alfalfa)
Clean tillage to accelerate residue breakdown
treatment: Fungicides are completely ineffective; bactericides are generally not economically viable or registered for field corn
organic_control: Sanitation of field equipment
Crop rotation
Residue destruction
chemical_control: Chemical options are ineffective and not recommended; do not apply fungicides for this bacterial disease
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain balanced crop nutrition to support overall plant vigor and minimize stress-induced susceptibility
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid running overhead irrigation during late afternoon or evening hours to limit the duration of continuous leaf moisture
monitoring: Scout fields mid-season, holding suspicious leaves up to the sun to check for wavy margins and translucent yellow halos
economic_importance: An emerging disease in many regions; currently causes minor to moderate yield impacts but presents operational challenges due to misdiagnosis as Gray Leaf Spot.
diagnosis_notes: Look for wavy, jagged margins on the lesions and a distinct yellow halo when backlit. Unlike Gray Leaf Spot, margins are NOT perfectly straight.

symptoms: Long, pale green-to-yellow linear lesions that follow leaf veins
Lesions turn brown, dry, and necrotic over time
Irregular feeding scars from the corn flea beetle are visible inside the lesions
Vascular wilting and stunting, particularly in young plants; stalk cavity may show brown discoloration
early_stage: Pale green or yellow streaks originating from flea beetle feeding marks on leaves
Slight wilting of seedling leaves during the heat of the day
advanced_stage: Extensive leaf drying, mimicking drought damage across the entire canopy
Systemic wilting, stunting, and death of young plants (wilt phase)
Main stalk produces an ooze of yellow bacterial droplets when cut
causes: Bacterium is vectored and carried inside the digestive tract of overwintering corn flea beetles
favorable_conditions: Mild winter temperatures (which allow high survival rates of the flea beetle vector)
spread_method: Vector transmission by the corn flea beetle (Chaetocnema pulicaria) during feeding
prevention: Plant highly resistant corn hybrids
Use systemic insecticidal seed treatments to control the flea beetle vector early in the season
Monitor winter temperatures to predict vector pressure via the Stevens-Castor model
treatment: No curative treatment for systemically infected plants; target the insect vector early
organic_control: Using resistant varieties is the primary organic management strategy
Row covers on small scales to exclude beetles
chemical_control: Apply insecticides to control flea beetles early in the season if winter models predict high vector survival and susceptible lines are grown; follow local regulations
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain adequate plant vigor; avoid extreme structural stress on seedlings
irrigation_recommendations: Provide adequate moisture to seedlings to prevent compounding the wilt symptoms with true moisture stress
monitoring: Count flea beetles on young seedlings (V1-V4 stage); treat if populations exceed economic thresholds (e.g., 5 beetles per plant on susceptible inbreds)
economic_importance: Historically highly destructive to sweet corn and seed corn inbreds; well managed in commercial field corn via resistance, but remains a critical quarantine concern for seed export.
diagnosis_notes: Look for the long yellow streaks that always contain tiny, dark flea beetle feeding scars inside the lesion pathway.

pathogen: Dickeya zeae Samson et al. (syn. Pectobacterium chrysanthemi pv. zeae)
symptoms: Rapid collapse and lodging of the plant mid-season, often at a single node
Infected stalk tissue becomes soft, water-soaked, and slimy
A foul, putrid, disagreeable odor emanates from the rotting tissue
The top leaves wilt and die rapidly, turning a slimy brown at the base
early_stage: Water-soaked appearance of the leaf sheath and stalk around a node
Slight soft texture when the node is compressed
advanced_stage: Complete structural twisting and collapse of the stalk
Internal pith completely turns into a foul-smelling liquid mush
Rapid drying and death of the entire plant within days of collapse
causes: Bacterial cells enter through natural openings, hydathodes, or wounds, often carried by irrigation water pooling in the whorl
favorable_conditions: Heavy rainfall or continuous overhead sprinkler irrigation from surface water sources
spread_method: Water splash, flooding, and overhead irrigation using contaminated surface water; insect wounding
prevention: Ensure excellent field drainage to prevent water accumulation
Avoid using stagnant surface pond water for overhead pivot irrigation
Select hybrids with structural tolerance
Clean equipment thoroughly
treatment: No effective chemical or biological treatments exist once stalk rot symptoms become visible
organic_control: Proper field drainage engineering
Crop rotation with non-hosts
Sanitating machinery
chemical_control: No registered, economically effective bactericides or chemicals exist for field crops; do not apply fungicides
nutrition_recommendations: Avoid over-application of nitrogen which leads to rapid, soft, succulent tissue development that bacteria easily penetrate
irrigation_recommendations: Critically important: Do not over-irrigate; manage sprinklers to avoid water accumulation in the plant whorls, especially during hot weather
monitoring: Scout fields during hot, humid mid-summer stretches; look for randomly collapsing plants and confirm via the distinctive foul odor
economic_importance: Can cause high localized losses in specific fields with poor drainage or those utilizing infested surface water under overhead pivots, though rare on a broad geographic scale.
diagnosis_notes: The rapid soft collapse at a node combined with an intensely foul, putrid odor is completely diagnostic for bacterial stalk rot.

pathogen: Pythium ultimum Trow; Pythium arrhenomanes Drechsler; and other Pythium species
symptoms: Damping-off of seedlings, causing collapse before or shortly after emergence
Roots appear water-soaked, soft, and dark brown to black
The outer root cortex sloughs off easily, leaving the inner vascular thread
Stunted vegetative growth, leaf yellowing, and uneven stand density
early_stage: Delayed or uneven seedling emergence across wet areas of the field
Slight yellowing and tip burn of early seedling leaves
advanced_stage: Complete destruction of the primary and secondary root systems
Seedlings rot off completely at the soil line
Surviving plants remain severely stunted, unproductive, and prone to early lodging
causes: Oomycete (water mold) structures (oospores) persist indefinitely in soil and germinate under saturated conditions
favorable_conditions: Cold soil temperatures (10-15°C) for certain species during planting, or warm wet soils for others
spread_method: Motile zoospores swim through water films in the soil to infect root tips
prevention: Use seed treated with targeted oomycete-specific fungicides
Improve field drainage and eliminate low-lying wet spots
Avoid planting into cold, waterlogged soils; delay until soils warm and dry structurally
treatment: No post-emergence curative treatment; rescue options do not exist for infected roots
organic_control: Controlled strip-tillage to warm up seedbeds
Installing tile drainage
Using high-vigor seed lots
chemical_control: Apply specific oomycete-targeted seed treatments prior to planting; standard fungal treatments are ineffective. Adhere to regional regulations
nutrition_recommendations: Apply a balanced starter fertilizer high in phosphorus close to the seed row to stimulate rapid root escape growth
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid pre-emergence over-irrigation; manage irrigation schedules strictly to prevent water saturation and pooling in fields
monitoring: Dig up stunted, chlorotic seedlings in low-lying, wet areas during the first 4 weeks post-planting; wash roots to check for sloughing cortex
economic_importance: A major driver of poor plant stands, requiring expensive replanting operations and causing significant early yield potential reduction due to uneven crop competition.
diagnosis_notes: Identified by dark, water-soaked roots where the outer cortex easily slips off the vascular core, combined with waterlogged soil history.
references: Ohio State University Extension Agronomy Guides

pathogen: Fusarium verticillioides (Sacc.) Nirenberg; Fusarium proliferatum (Matsush.) Nirenberg
symptoms: Internal pith of the stalk disintegrates and displays a whitish-pink to salmon discoloration
Lower internodes become soft, easily crushed by finger pressure
Leaves turn dull grayish-green prematurely, resembling frost damage
Stalk lodging occurs near the base of the plant prior to harvest
early_stage: Premature wilting and drying of the upper leaves late in the grain fill period
Slight softening of the lowest stalk internodes
advanced_stage: Complete stringy disintegration of the internal stalk pith, leaving only the vascular strands
Distinct pinkish-salmon tint inside the stalk
Widespread lodging across the field, especially under high winds
causes: Fungus enters through the roots or wounds and colonizes the stalk systemically, accelerating when the plant draws down stalk carbohydrates
favorable_conditions: Drought stress or cloudiness during grain fill followed by wet weather
Any factor reducing photosynthesis (leaf blights, insect feeding)
spread_method: Soil-borne inoculum and crop residue conidia entering through root systems or stalk wounds
prevention: Select hybrids with excellent stalk strength and disease resistance packages
Avoid excessively high plant populations that increase competition and stress
Control leaf diseases to maintain photosynthetic capacity
treatment: Foliar fungicides applied at VT/R1 can help indirectly by preserving leaf health and reducing carbohydrate stress
organic_control: Balanced crop rotation
Proper plant spacing to reduce individual plant stress
Residue incorporation
chemical_control: No direct curative chemical treatment for the stalk interior; management focuses on preventative agronomy and hybrid selection
recommended_insecticides: Insecticides targeting stalk-boring insects to eliminate structural entry wounds
nutrition_recommendations: Ensure strict balance between Nitrogen and Potassium; avoid excessive N paired with deficient K, which severely weakens stalk rinds
irrigation_recommendations: Provide steady, uniform irrigation throughout the reproductive and grain-fill stages to prevent carbohydrate cannibalization from the stalk
monitoring: Conduct the pinch or push test on lower internodes of 100 consecutive plants at mid-to-late grain fill to evaluate stalk integrity
economic_importance: Highly significant contributor to harvest losses and mechanical harvesting difficulties due to stalk lodging and ear drop globally.
diagnosis_notes: Look for the whitish-pink or salmon-pink coloration inside the shredded stalk pith, lacking the dark black external streaks of Anthracnose.
references: Purdue University Extension Field Crop Manuals

symptoms: Internal stalk pith breaks down, leaving vascular bundles covered in millions of microscopic black specks (microsclerotia)
The internal stalk takes on a distinct grayish-black, charcoal-like appearance
Premature ripening and drying of the plant
Stalk lodging and structural collapse near the soil line
early_stage: Premature drying of upper leaves, turning streaks of light brown during late grain fill
Roots show small, dark, water-soaked streaks
advanced_stage: Lower internodes are completely hollowed out and black inside, resembling charcoal dust
Rind becomes extremely brittle and breaks easily at the base
Microsclerotia can be scraped off internal fibers
causes: Fungus survives for many years in the soil or residue as highly resilient microsclerotia
favorable_conditions: Hot (above 30-35°C) and extremely dry weather during the reproductive and grain filling stages
spread_method: Soil-borne microsclerotia germinate and penetrate root tissues directly during periods of heat and moisture stress
prevention: Select drought-tolerant hybrids with strong lodging resistance scores
Implement conservation tillage or mulch to conserve soil moisture and lower soil temperatures
Avoid overly high plant densities in non-irrigated fields
treatment: Chemical applications are completely ineffective; management relies entirely on moisture preservation and hybrid selection
organic_control: Crop rotation with non-hosts for 2+ years
Applying organic mulches or cover crops to retain soil moisture
chemical_control: No registered or effective chemical fungicides exist for Charcoal Rot in field corn
recommended_biological_control: Trichoderma harzianum strains as a soil amendment
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain optimal potassium levels to support osmotic regulation and improve drought tolerance within the plant
irrigation_recommendations: Critically important: Maintain adequate irrigation during and after pollination to prevent the severe drought stress that triggers Charcoal Rot development
monitoring: Scout hot, dry fields close to harvest; split open the lower 20 cm of stalks on wilted plants to check for the charcoal-like dust appearance
economic_importance: Can cause serious localized yield losses and severe lodging in semi-arid, hot corn-growing regions under dryland management.
diagnosis_notes: The absolute presence of millions of tiny black microsclerotia inside the disintegrated stalk, giving it a gray-black charcoal look, is definitive.

symptoms: Finely mottled mosaic pattern of alternating light-green and dark-green patches on leaves
Symptoms are most pronounced on young, expanding leaves
Infected plants may display severe stunting if infected as seedlings
Poor ear development, reduced seed set, and occasional reddish coloration of leaves late in the season
early_stage: Small chlorotic spots or flecks forming broken linear stripes on the youngest leaves
Slightly lighter green overall canopy color
advanced_stage: Classic intense green/yellow mosaic pattern across all foliage
Severe shortening of internodes (stunting)
Barren stalks or poorly filled ears with distorted kernel rows
causes: Virus is transmitted from overwintering perennial grass hosts (especially Johnsongrass) to corn by aphid vectors
favorable_conditions: Proximity to large stands of infected Johnsongrass or other wild perennial grasses
Early planting dates coinciding with vector flights
spread_method: Vector transmission by more than 20 species of aphids (e.g., Rhopalosiphum maidis) in a non-persistent manner; can be mechanically transmitted
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids
Eradicate Johnsongrass and perennial wild grasses within and around field borders
Manage planting windows to avoid peak aphid migration times
treatment: There is no direct curative chemical treatment for viral diseases once a plant is infected
organic_control: Rigorous weed management around fields to eliminate viral reservoirs
Selecting resistant seed lines
chemical_control: Insecticides targeting aphids are generally ineffective at preventing transmission because non-persistent transmission occurs within seconds of probing; follow local guidelines
nutrition_recommendations: Ensure standard balanced nutrition to support plant vigor, though it will not cure or halt the viral progression
irrigation_recommendations: Provide adequate water to reduce compound stress on stunted, virus-infected root systems
monitoring: Scout early vegetative corn, examining the whorl and newest leaves for fine mottling, while checking for the presence of aphids
economic_importance: Historically significant, but currently well controlled via commercial hybrid resistance; remains a threat where susceptible lines are close to infected wild grasses.
diagnosis_notes: Look for the fine, dark and light green mosaic mottling on the youngest leaves, often originating near wild grass reservoirs.

symptoms: Fine chlorotic spots that coalesce into extensive yellow streaks along leaf veins
Mild to severe leaf chlorosis and drying starting from the margins
Shortened internodes leading to notable plant stunting
Malformed, small, or completely barren ears with severe kernel abortion
early_stage: Delicate, faint chlorotic speckling on the leaves
Slight pale green appearance of the whorl
advanced_stage: Widespread bright yellow chlorosis across the foliage
Leaf necrosis starting at the tips and moving inward
Severe plant stunting and direct synergy with potyviruses to cause lethal necrosis
causes: Virus is introduced and spread within fields by chrysomelid beetle vectors and contaminated seed lots
favorable_conditions: High populations of beetle vectors (corn rootworms, flea beetles)
spread_method: Vector transmission by corn rootworm beetles (Diabrotica spp.), flea beetles, and thrips; low rate of seed transmission
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant hybrids if available locally
Implement strict crop rotation out of corn for 2 years to break vector cycles
Use certified disease-free clean seed stocks
treatment: There is no direct curative chemical treatment for viral diseases once a plant is infected
organic_control: Strict crop rotation away from all grass crops
Managing vector populations using organic traps or botanical sprays
chemical_control: Vector management through targeted insecticidal seed treatments or foliar sprays against adult beetles may help reduce secondary spread; follow local laws
nutrition_recommendations: Maintain adequate balanced fertilizer applications to support structural growth under viral pressure
irrigation_recommendations: Maintain consistent irrigation to minimize environmental stress that accelerates viral leaf drying
monitoring: Scout fields regularly for unexplained leaf yellowing and stunting, checking closely for rootworm or flea beetle feeding damage
economic_importance: Highly important independently, but critically dangerous as the indispensable component of Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN), which causes devastating food security failures.
diagnosis_notes: Characterized by fine chlorotic mottling that transitions into widespread margin-first leaf yellowing and stunting, coupled with vector presence.
references: CIMMYT Maize Lethal Necrosis Management Guides

pathogen: Co-infection of Maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV) AND a Potyvirus (e.g., Maize dwarf mosaic virus - MDMV, or Sugarcane mosaic virus - SCMV)
symptoms: Severe, rapid yellowing and drying of leaves starting from the margins moving inward
Dead heart symptom where the inner whorl dies and dries up completely
Extreme stunting of the entire plant with shortened internodes
Ears are completely barren, deformed, or contain zero grain set; premature death of the entire plant
early_stage: Intense chlorotic mottling and yellowing of the young leaves
Severe growth lag compared to healthy plants
advanced_stage: Complete necrosis and death of the vegetative whorl (dead heart)
The entire field takes on a scorched, brown, dead appearance before flowering
Total crop failure with zero harvestable grain
causes: Synergistic co-infection when a single corn plant is simultaneously infected by both MCMV and a grass-infecting potyvirus
favorable_conditions: High populations of mixed vectors (aphids, thrips, and beetles) year-round
Presence of alternative grass hosts near fields
spread_method: Combined vector transmission: aphids transmit the potyvirus; thrips and beetles transmit MCMV. Can also spread via contaminated seed rows
prevention: Plant specifically bred MLN-resistant hybrids
Enforce a strict community-wide host-free period or crop rotation break away from corn
Control alternative grass weeds rigorously
Use certified clean seed
treatment: There is no direct curative chemical treatment for viral diseases; infected plants must be removed or destroyed
organic_control: Enforcing strict crop rotation and synchronous planting dates across regions
Immediate roguing and burning of early infected plants
chemical_control: No chemical curative options exist. Intense vector control using registered insecticides may be used defensively but rarely prevents primary infection; follow local mandates
recommended_insecticides: Systemic insecticidal seed treatments and targeted foliar sprays to suppress thrips, beetles, and aphids
nutrition_recommendations: Fertilization is ineffective at preventing or mitigating MLN; focus entirely on resistance and exclusion
irrigation_recommendations: Irrigation cannot save MLN-infected plants; prioritize water conservation or healthy sections
monitoring: Scout fields weekly post-emergence; instantly report and isolate areas showing rapid margin necrosis and whorl death
economic_importance: Catastrophic economic and food security impact, particularly in East Africa, where it has caused complete crop failure and massive local economic damage.
diagnosis_notes: Identified by the extreme synergy of symptoms: rapid margin-inward drying, dead hearts, complete stunting, and total ear barrenness.

pathogen: Peronosclerospora sorghi (Weston & Uppal) C.G. Shaw; and other Peronosclerospora species
symptoms: Distinct vivid chlorotic stripes running parallel along the leaf blade
A white, downy, furry fungal-like growth appears on the lower leaf surface under humid conditions
Infected leaves become narrow, erect, thickened, and brittle
Deformed reproductive structures, including 'crazy top' (phyllody of the tassel) and barren ears
early_stage: Systemically infected seedlings emerge pale green to yellow and stunted
Appearance of long, light-green to yellow bands extending from the leaf base
advanced_stage: Chlorotic stripes turn brown and necrotic, leaf blades shred longitudinally
Tassel transforms into a mass of distorted leafy structures (crazy top)
Ears are completely barren or replaced by leafy growths, resulting in no grain production
causes: Oomycete pathogen overwinters as oospores in the soil or spreads via wind-blown conidia from infected alternative hosts (sorghum, wild grasses)
favorable_conditions: Warm night temperatures (20-25°C) paired with heavy morning dews
Saturated soils during early seedling stages
spread_method: Soil-borne oospores infect roots systemically; airborne conidia produced at night spread the disease to leaves during humid conditions
prevention: Plant highly resistant corn hybrids adapted to the region
Use systemic oomycete-targeted seed treatments
Implement crop rotation with non-grass crops
Eradicate wild sorghum species near fields
treatment: Foliar fungicide treatments are rarely effective or economical; prevention via seed treatment is vital
organic_control: Deep plowing to bury soil oospores deeply
Strict crop rotation out of susceptible grasses
Early roguing of systematically infected chlorotic seedlings
chemical_control: Apply registered systemic oomycete-specific seed treatments prior to planting; comply with all local agricultural regulations
nutrition_recommendations: Provide balanced starter fertilizers to promote rapid early growth, enabling seedlings to outpace systemic infection vulnerability
irrigation_recommendations: Avoid waterlogging fields post-planting; schedule irrigation to prevent prolonged leaf wetness during warm nights
monitoring: Scout fields 3-6 weeks after planting, looking for distinctly pale, striped, erect leaves and looking beneath leaves for the white fuzzy growth
economic_importance: Highly important in tropical and subtropical regions (e.g., Southeast Asia, parts of Africa and the Americas), where it can cause up to 100% yield loss in susceptible fields.
diagnosis_notes: Look for the long parallel chlorotic stripes, the signature fuzzy downy white growth underneath the leaves, and leaf shredding.
